St. Job of Pochaev

Saints

St. Job of Pochaev

St. Ivan Zhelezo · John, great-schema name

Period
Circa 1551–1651 in the selected lives
Region
Galicia, Dubno, Pochaev
Titles / vocation
Venerable · Abbot · Confessor
Commemoration
October 28

Introduction

St. Job of Pochaev is remembered as an abbot, ascetic, and defender of Orthodox communities after the Union of Brest. His life combines solitary prayer with building, publishing, and practical care for the monastery.

Read the published life [1]

Death / martyrdom

Peaceful repose in 1651 after long monastic service

Read circumstances and sources

Background

Born St. Ivan Zhelezo in Galicia, he enters the Ugornits monastery as a child and receives tonsure with the name St. Job. Prince Constantine Ostrozhsky later asks him to lead the Holy Cross monastery near Dubno.

[1] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 1, 2

The ACROD account places his formation within Orthodox family life and a monastery entered at ten. It follows his early tonsure, priestly ordination, and two decades of leadership at Dubno. The regional setting includes pressure on Orthodox institutions and a struggle to sustain instruction and worship.

[2] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 80, 81, 82

Life and notable events

At Pochaev he is elected abbot and works with the brethren in gardens and waterworks. The OCA links his defense of Orthodoxy with copying and distributing books and notes his presence at the Kiev council of 1628.

[1] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 3, 4, 5

The diocesan article describes a cave used for withdrawal and prayer beside the demands of common life. It also follows disputes over the monastery’s property and the dangers faced by the brotherhood. Miraculous light in the cave is attributed to the life and its named disciple-witness, rather than independently demonstrated here.

[2] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 85, 86, 87, 88, 90, 91, 92

Death and martyrdom

The OCA dates his repose to 1651 after more than fifty years directing Pochaev. It does not say he was killed. It records the uncovering of his relics in 1659 and again in 1833.

[1] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 6, 7

The diocesan narrative gives October 28 for his repose after the Liturgy and says he dies peacefully. Its extraordinary lifespan and foreknowledge of death remain elements of the hagiographical account.

[2] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 94

Writings and legacy

Both accounts remember the defense of Orthodox teaching through books and pastoral work. The diocesan article places Pochaev within the memory of several neighboring peoples; its polemical reading of regional church conflict remains an identified Orthodox interpretation. It should not be mistaken for the beliefs of every contemporary Catholic or Protestant.

[2] Published ecclesiastical life or account · Published life, selected article paragraphs 80, 82, 92

And he spake this parable unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others:

Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican.

The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican.

I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.

And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner.

I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.

[3] Public-domain Bible translation · Luke 18:9–14
